1.pericope_label: A door standing open in heaven

schools.summary: Gill insists the seeing was with the eyes of the mind, the reason prophets are called seers.
Henry draws the lesson that what is done on earth is first settled in heaven and that we may not intrude into that secret until called up to it.

Ellicott and Robertson read the perfect participle to mean the door already stood open, Robertson adding that the opening phrase marks a change of panorama rather than chronology; Barnes weighs the competing accounts of what John actually saw and denies that any representation to the bodily eye need be supposed.
Wesley makes "after these things" the structural divider of the prophecy and traces a widening series of openings through the book; Clarke takes the door as a visible aperture in the sky.
Victorinus reads the open door as the new covenant laid open at the ascension, and argues from the sameness of the voice that the speaker in the prophets and the speaker in the Gospel are one.

debates: Whether John saw with the bodily eye: Clarke calls it a visible aperture in the sky, while Gill, Henry and Barnes all place the seeing in the mind or spirit.
Whether "after these things" marks temporal sequence or only a change of scene, Robertson holding for the latter.
outliers: Clarke stands alone in describing a literal opening in the sky over John’s head.

2.pericope_label: The throne set in heaven and the One upon it

schools.summary: Gill supposes John had lapsed from his ecstasy and now returned to it, and describes the jasper from the high priest’s breastplate as a variegated, spotted stone.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson agree the throne stood already set, deny that the scene is the Jerusalem temple, and read the unnamed occupant as a deliberate guard against image-making; they divide sharply over the colour of the jasper.

Wesley makes the throne the centre from which all things proceed and to which they return, and reads the stones emblematically as purity, justice and favour; Clarke stresses that the glory, not the person, is described.

debates: The colour and identity of the jasper: Barnes infers princely red, Wesley glittering white, Gill green spotted with red, Ellicott a crystal-clear stone distinct from ordinary jasper, and Robertson declines to fix it at all.
Whether "I was in the Spirit" marks a new rapture (Gill) or the continuance of the one begun earlier (Robertson).
Whether the vision is set in heaven itself or in the temple at Jerusalem, which Barnes reports and rejects.
outliers: Robertson warns that the whole scene is imagery rather than a description of objects actually in heaven.
Wesley uses the throne to argue that theological and historical readings of the book must be joined rather than chosen between.

4.pericope_label: The four and twenty elders enthroned

schools.summary: Gill sets the seats in a semicircle answering the rainbow and compares the seating of the Jewish council, while admitting the numbers do not match.

Barnes and Ellicott both insist the elders sit on thrones rather than seats and read them as the redeemed Church in triumph, drawn from every nation; Robertson notes the textual variation and refuses to decide why the number is twenty-four.

Clarke traces the number to the lesser Sanhedrin or the twenty-four priestly courses and reads the raiment as priestly; Wesley takes the elders for the saints of former ages and infers from their never being called souls that they already have glorified bodies.

debates: The source of the number twenty-four: the lesser Sanhedrin (Gill, Clarke), the priestly courses of David (Clarke, Ellicott), the tribes joined to the apostles or the two Testaments (Ellicott), or nothing that can be determined (Robertson).
Whether the elders are human at all: Barnes, Ellicott and Wesley take them for the redeemed Church, while Robertson leaves open that they are an unknown rank of angels.
Whether "seats" or "thrones" is the right rendering, Barnes and Ellicott both faulting the received translation.
outliers: Wesley alone argues from the absence of the word "souls" that the elders are already embodied.
Ellicott observes that Ezekiel’s parallel vision contains no human figures, making the elders a deliberate addition here.

5.pericope_label: Lightnings from the throne and the seven lamps of fire

schools.summary: Ellicott, Robertson and Barnes read the storm as the abiding token of divine power rather than of imminent judgment, and take the seven torches for the Spirit of God burning perpetually before the throne; Ellicott adds that the bow, the torches and the thunder set three covenant signs together.

Wesley distributes the three phenomena among the senses and holds that what terrifies weak men is joy to heaven and protection to the saints; Clarke identifies the seven lamps as seven ministering angels rather than as the Spirit.

debates: Whether the seven lamps are the Holy Spirit in His sevenfold operation, as Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson hold, or seven attendant angels, as Clarke states.
Whether the lightnings and thunderings announce judgments about to fall or only display the power by which God judges, Ellicott arguing for the latter against an unnamed party of interpreters.
outliers: Ellicott alone connects the torches with the fire that passed between the pieces in the covenant with Abraham.
Wesley reverses the usual effect of the storm, making it a source of pleasure to the inhabitants of heaven.

6.pericope_label: The sea of glass and the four living creatures

schools.summary: Gill eliminates the proposed identifications one by one and refuses to make the sea stand for the world, since the world is never figured as a still sea.

Barnes and Robertson describe the sea as a transparent expanse and probably the pavement of the throne; Ellicott opposes it to the stormy waters on which the harlot sits and reads it as the settled counsels of God; all three reject the rendering "beasts" and take the creatures as symbolic, Barnes following Ezekiel and Robertson making them creation over against the redeemed.

Wesley identifies the sea with the Spirit of God under the emblem of water and makes the living creatures the Christian church over against a Jewish eldership; Clarke attacks the word "beasts" and traces it to Wiclif.

debates: What the sea of glass represents: the pavement of the throne (Barnes), the counsels of God (Ellicott), the Spirit of God (Wesley), or none of the identifications commonly offered (Gill).
How the living creatures stand in relation to the throne, where Barnes puts them beneath it, Ellicott beyond the sea, Robertson one on each side, and Wesley at the four quarters.
What the living creatures represent: the majesty and government of God (Barnes), created nature over against the redeemed (Robertson), or the Christian church over against the Jewish (Wesley).
outliers: Wesley reads the sea, the seven torches and the later river of life as one emblem of the Spirit.
Wesley here assigns the elders to the Jewish church, a narrower account than the one he gives of them earlier in the chapter.

7.pericope_label: The four faces: lion, calf, man and eagle

schools.summary: Gill makes the lion an emblem of the ministers of the word, strong to endure and bold to preach.

Robertson and Barnes agree the likeness reaches only to the face and that the bodies were uniform; Robertson takes the four for what is noblest and swiftest in nature and rejects the evangelist scheme, Barnes reads them as attributes of divine government, and Ellicott makes them representatives of animated nature whose qualities compose a picture of true service.

Clarke reports both the tribal standards of the Israelite camp and the traditional assignment of the four to the evangelists, and makes the creatures the Christian Church; Wesley compares the cherubim of Ezekiel and of the mercy seat.

debates: Whether the four faces answer to the four evangelists, which Clarke transmits as Christian tradition and Robertson calls an early and baseless identification.
What the creatures represent: animated nature (Ellicott), the attributes of God’s government (Barnes), the Christian Church (Clarke), or the ministers of the word (Gill).
What the multitude of eyes signifies, Ellicott rejecting unceasing praise in favour of reason and vigilance stamped on the power of nature.
outliers: Wesley passes on, without adopting it, a reading of the cherubim as emblems of the Trinity and the incarnation.
Barnes supports the calf-emblem with a long excursus on bull worship in Egypt and the winged bulls excavated at Nineveh.

8.pericope_label: Six wings, unresting eyes, and the threefold holy

schools.summary: Gill assigns the three pairs of wings to reverence, a confessed sense of imperfection, and readiness to serve.
Henry hears in the threefold holy the adoration of one God in Father, Son and Spirit, and identifies the glory Isaiah saw as Christ’s.

Barnes reattaches "about" to the eyes and reads them as universal providential vigilance, declining to reconstruct the wings; Robertson traces the number of wings to Isaiah and makes the unresting activity of nature a perpetual tribute; Ellicott notes a manuscript that repeats "holy" eight times and the absence of Isaiah’s closing clause, and rejects a reading that would make the creatures God’s creative power rather than His creation.

Wesley derives the meaning of "holy" from separation and makes holiness and Godhead equivalent, explaining the missing clause about the earth as deferred until the glory fills it; Clarke supplies rabbinic parallels for the whole scene and reads the creatures as representatives of the whole creation.

debates: What the covered feet signify: a sense of sinfulness and imperfection (Gill), modesty or humility (Barnes, Ellicott), or readiness and diligence (Wesley).
Whether the living creatures represent the creative power of God or created things themselves, Ellicott reporting the first view and adopting the second.
outliers: Clarke quotes a rabbinic saying that man, eagle, ox and lion hold principality in the world, which is the same fourfold scheme Ellicott had already used on the previous verse without attributing it.
Wesley explains the absence of Isaiah’s "the whole earth is full of his glory" as a deliberate deferral until the end of the book.

9.pericope_label: The elders fall down and cast their crowns

schools.summary: Gill keeps the living creatures for the ministers who lead worship and the elders for the church members who follow, and finds the persons of the Trinity glorified in election, redemption and sanctification.
Henry draws the pattern of heavenly praise into a rule for praise on earth: constant, united, thankful and humble.

Robertson takes the clause as one of repetition and pairs created nature with the redeemed in a single act of worship, while noting that some make the elders angels; Barnes reads the repeated praise as the church answering each fresh display of God’s government, and the crowns as an acknowledgment that the triumph was His gift.

Wesley has the elders fall at the very instant the creatures speak, and distinguishes the creatures’ indirect ascription from the elders’ direct address; Clarke explains the casting of crowns from eastern prostration and the homage of subject kings.

debates: Whether the elders are redeemed men or angels, a view Robertson reports from a modern editor without endorsing it.
What the living creatures and elders respectively stand for: nature and the redeemed (Robertson), the government of God and His church (Barnes), or ministers and church members (Gill).
outliers: Wesley observes that the living creatures speak of God in the third person while the elders address Him directly, and connects this to their different postures.

11.pericope_label: Worthy art thou: the doxology of creation

schools.summary: Gill prefers the longer reading "O Lord, and our God" and explains that God receives glory only in the sense that creatures confess it to be His.

Ellicott sets the doxology out as a threefold ascription and insists the clause reads "they were" rather than "they are"; Robertson supports this from the grammar, treating the nominative as a vocative and allowing that the imperfect may point to a potential existence in God’s purpose before creation in time; Barnes argues that the universe exists for no other reason than the will of God and that created things were formed from nothing.

Wesley matches the threefold ascription to the threefold holy and reads the closing clause as continuance in being; Clarke infers from "for thy pleasure" that God hates nothing He has made and could not have created any intelligent being for eternal misery.

debates: Whether the text reads "O Lord" or the longer "O Lord and our God", where Gill and Ellicott both cite the wider manuscript support for the longer form.

Whether the clause says that all things "are" or that they "were", and what the imperfect implies: Ellicott insists on the past, Robertson entertains a pre-temporal existence in the divine purpose, and Wesley reads a beginning followed by continuance.
Whether the doxology bears on the destiny of creatures, Clarke arguing from it against any eternal misery decreed in the making, in a chapter where Gill has the elders praise God for election.
outliers: Clarke uses the verse polemically, calling it high time that the benevolence of God were vindicated from the contrary supposition.
Wesley holds that God receives this praise also in the destruction of His enemies.
